_: English meaning written for this library (en-scriptures): one to three plain sentences per mantra, faithful to the words, following the traditional reading (Śaṅkara). [meaning, [footnotes]]
shanti.1: Om. May he (the Lord) protect us both (teacher and student) together. May he nourish us both together. May we both gain strength together. May what we both have studied be full of light. May we never hate each other. Om, peace, peace, peace.

The śānti mantra of the Upaniṣads of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, recited by teacher and student together. Peace is said three times: for the three kinds of affliction, from within oneself, from other beings and from the gods (fate).
1.1.1: Om. Desiring (the fruit of the sacrifice), the son of Vājaśravas gave away all his possessions (in the Viśvajit sacrifice). He had a son named Naciketā.
Uśan is read with Śaṅkara as 'desiring'; some take it as the sage's name (Uśan Vājaśravas). The father is also called Gautama and Auddālaki Āruṇi (1.1.10–11).
1.1.2: While the cows given as the sacrificial fee were being led away (to the priests), faith (concern for his father's good) entered the boy, and he thought:
1.1.3: Naciketā thought: These cows have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk, and are barren now. Joyless are the worlds to which he goes who gives these as gifts.
1.1.4: He said to his father: Father, to whom will you give me? A second and a third time (he asked), and the father said to him: To Death I give you.
The father said it in anger; Naciketā took it as said. In a sacrifice of all one owns, he thought himself too among the things to be given.
1.1.5: Naciketā thought: Among many (pupils or sons) I go as the first, among many as the middling (never the last). What task of Yama is there that will be done through me today?
1.1.6: (Father,) look back at how our forefathers were, and look ahead: others (the good) are the same (none went back on his word). A mortal ripens like corn and like corn is born again.
Naciketā urges his father to keep his word: life is passing in any case. The father then sent him to Yama's house.
1.1.7: A brāhmaṇa guest enters a house like the fire Vaiśvānara; (householders) offer him this appeasement (the welcome of water for the feet and the rest). O Vaivasvata (Yama), fetch water (for him).
Yama was away for three days; on his return his household (or his ministers) said this to him. Naciketā had sat at his door three nights without eating.
1.1.8: Hope and expectation (their fruits), the company of the good and kindly true speech (their fruits), sacrifices and works of public good (their fruits), and sons and cattle — all this a brāhmaṇa staying unfed in a house destroys for the man of little understanding in whose house he stays.
1.1.9: Yama said: O brāhmaṇa, a guest worthy of reverence, you have stayed three nights in my house without eating. Salutation to you, O brāhmaṇa; may it be well with me. In return choose three boons.
1.1.10: Naciketā said: O Death, may my father Gautama be calm in mind towards me, glad and free of anger, and may he recognise me and speak to me (with love) when you have sent me back. This is the first of the three boons I choose.
1.1.11: Yama said: Released by me, Auddālaki Āruṇi (your father) will recognise you and be as before; seeing you freed from the mouth of death, he will sleep happily at night, his anger gone.
1.1.12: Naciketā said: In the world of heaven there is no fear; you (Death) are not there, and no one fears old age. Having crossed both hunger and thirst, gone beyond sorrow, one rejoices in the world of heaven.
1.1.13: O Death, you know that fire which leads to heaven; explain it to me, who have faith, (the fire by which) those in heaven attain immortality. This I choose by the second boon.
Immortality here is the long life of the gods, the fruit of rites and worship, which Death himself will later call impermanent (1.2.10).
1.1.14: Yama said: O Naciketā, I know that fire which leads to heaven well, and I tell it to you; learn it from me. Know this fire, which brings the endless world (heaven) and is the support (of the world), as seated in the cave (of the intellect of the wise).
1.1.15: (Yama) told him of the fire that is the source of the worlds: which bricks, how many, and how (they are to be laid). And he repeated it back exactly as it had been told. Then Death, pleased with him, spoke again:
1.1.16: The great-souled (Death), being pleased, said to him: Here today I give you one more boon. This fire will be known by your very name (the Naciketa fire); and take this many-formed necklace (a chain of jewels, or the many-formed course of works).
Sṛṅkā: in Śaṅkara's reading a necklace of jewels, or the knowledge of the many-formed course of works and their fruits.
1.1.17: He who has piled the Naciketa fire thrice, having come together with the three (mother, father and teacher; or Veda, Smṛti and the good), and performs the three works (sacrifice, study and charity), crosses birth and death. Knowing this god worthy of praise, born of Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha), the knower, and realising (him as himself), he attains the utmost peace.
1.1.18: He who, knowing these three (the bricks, their number and their manner), piles the Naciketa fire thrice with this knowledge, casts off the snares of death beforehand and, gone beyond sorrow, rejoices in the world of heaven.
1.1.19: O Naciketā, this is your fire that leads to heaven, which you chose by the second boon; people will call this fire yours. Now, Naciketā, choose the third boon.
1.1.20: Naciketā said: There is this doubt about a man who has died: some say he (the Self) exists, others that he does not. Taught by you, I would know this. This is the third of the boons.
1.1.21: Yama said: On this even the gods doubted of old; it is not easy to know, for this truth (the Self) is subtle. Choose another boon, Naciketā; do not press me on this, give it up.
1.1.22: Naciketā said: On this, O Death, even the gods doubted, and you too say it is not easy to know; but another teacher of it like you cannot be found, and no other boon is equal to this.
1.1.23: Yama said: Choose sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years; many cattle, elephants, gold and horses; choose a wide expanse of the earth (a kingdom), and live yourself as many years as you wish.
1.1.24: If you think of any boon equal to this, choose it: wealth and long life. Be (a king) on the wide earth, Naciketā; I make you the enjoyer of (all) desires.
1.1.25: Whatever enjoyments are hard to obtain in the world of mortals, ask for them all as you please. Here are fair women with chariots and musical instruments; such are not to be had by men. Be served by these whom I give you. But, Naciketā, do not ask about death.
1.1.26: Naciketā said: O Death, these last only till tomorrow, and they wear away the vigour of all a mortal's senses. Even the whole of life is short. Keep your chariots, your dance and song.
1.1.27: Man cannot be satisfied with wealth. Now that we have seen you, we shall get wealth (when we want it); and we shall live only as long as you allow. The boon I choose is that one alone (the knowledge of the Self).
1.1.28: Having come near the undecaying immortals and knowing (what is higher than their gifts), what mortal who grows old and lives below (on earth), reflecting on beauty, pleasure and delight, would take delight in a very long life?
1.1.29: O Death, tell us that about which people doubt, the great matter of the hereafter. Naciketā chooses no boon other than this one that has entered the hidden depth.
1.2.1: Yama said: The good is one thing and the pleasant quite another; with different ends, both bind a man. Of the two, it goes well with him who takes the good; he who chooses the pleasant falls from the goal.
1.2.2: The good and the pleasant both come to a man; the wise man examines them well and separates them. The wise man chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull man chooses the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping (the body and its comforts).
1.2.3: You, Naciketā, have considered the pleasant and pleasant-looking enjoyments and let them go. You have not taken this chain made of wealth, in which many men sink.
1.2.4: Far apart, opposed and leading to different ends are these two: what is known as ignorance and what is known as knowledge. I consider Naciketā one who seeks knowledge; the many enjoyments could not tempt you.
1.2.5: Living in the midst of ignorance, thinking themselves wise and learned, the deluded wander round and round, stumbling (through sorrows), like the blind led by a blind man.
1.2.6: The way to the hereafter does not occur to the childish, heedless man deluded by wealth. Thinking 'this world exists, there is no other', he comes again and again under my sway.
1.2.7: He (the Self) whom many cannot even get to hear of, whom many cannot know even when hearing — rare is the teacher of him, skilful (and rare) is he who attains him, and rare is he who knows him, taught by a skilful teacher.
1.2.8: Taught by an inferior man, this (Self) cannot be well understood, being thought of in many ways. Taught by one who is at one with it, there is no doubt about it here; it is subtler than the subtlest measure and beyond reasoning.
1.2.9: This understanding is not to be reached by reasoning, dearest; taught by another (a knower of the Self), it leads to true knowledge. You have gained it; ah, you are truly steadfast. May we have a questioner like you, Naciketā.
1.2.10: I know that the treasure (won by works) is impermanent, for the permanent is not won by impermanent means. Yet I piled the Naciketa fire and, by impermanent things, attained the (relatively) lasting (state of Yama).
1.2.11: The fulfilment of desire, the support of the world, the endless fruit of rites, the far shore of fearlessness, the praiseworthy, great and widely sung state (of Hiraṇyagarbha), and your own standing — having seen all this, Naciketā, you wisely and firmly let it go.
1.2.12: Hard to see, entered into the hidden depth, seated in the cave (of the heart), dwelling in the thicket (of the world), ancient — knowing that shining one (the Self) by attaining the yoga of the inner Self, the wise man leaves joy and sorrow behind.
The yoga of the inner Self: withdrawing the mind from outer objects and fixing it within, on the Self.
1.2.13: Having heard this and grasped it well, having drawn out this subtle one, the very nature of truth, (from the body) and attained it, a mortal rejoices, for he has found what is to be delighted in. I think the house (of Brahman) stands open for Naciketā.
1.2.14: Naciketā said: That which you see as apart from right and apart from wrong, apart from this done and not done (effect and cause), apart from the past and the future — tell me that.
1.2.15: Yama said: The goal which all the Vedas declare, which all austerities speak of, desiring which men live the life of a student of Brahman — that goal I tell you in brief: it is Om.
1.2.16: This syllable indeed is Brahman; this syllable indeed is the supreme. Knowing this syllable, whatever one wishes, that is his.
1.2.17: This support is the best; this support is the supreme. Knowing this support, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.
1.2.18: The knowing one (the Self) is not born, nor does it die; it did not come from anything, nor did anything come from it. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.
1.2.19: If the killer thinks he kills it, and if the killed thinks it is killed, both of them do not understand: it neither kills nor is killed.
1.2.20: Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, the Self is seated in the heart of this creature. One free of desire sees that glory of the Self through the serenity of the senses and the mind, and is freed from sorrow.
1.2.21: Sitting, it travels far; lying down, it goes everywhere. Who but I can know that shining one, who is joyful and joyless (both)?

It travels while sitting and goes everywhere while lying down: the Self is itself motionless and all-pervading; the movement is of the mind and the body. Joyful and joyless: it is in every state and bound by none.
1.2.22: Knowing the Self as bodiless among bodies, abiding among the unstable, great and all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve.
1.2.23: This Self is not attained by discourse, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. It is attained by him alone whom it chooses; to him this Self reveals its own form.
Śaṅkara: the seeker who longs for this Self alone is the one who attains it.
1.2.24: Not one who has not turned away from bad conduct, not the unquiet (who does not control his senses), not the unconcentrated, nor one whose mind is not at peace, can attain it even by knowledge.
1.2.25: He for whom the brāhmaṇas and the warriors both become food, and death is the sauce — who truly knows where he (the Self) is?
1.3.1: Two (the individual self and the supreme Self), drinking the fruit of good deeds (in the world), have entered the cave (of the heart), the higher half of the supreme (Brahman). The knowers of Brahman, the keepers of the five fires (householders) and those who have piled the Naciketa fire thrice call them (as different as) shade and sunlight.
The supreme Self enjoys no fruit; the two are together, so both are called drinkers, as all who walk with umbrella-bearers are called 'the umbrella people' (Śaṅkara).
1.3.2: That which is the bridge for the sacrificers, and the supreme imperishable Brahman, the fearless far shore for those who wish to cross (the ocean of the world) — may we be able (to kindle) the Naciketa fire.
1.3.3: Know the Self as the lord of the chariot and the body as the chariot; know the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins.
1.3.4: The senses, they say, are the horses, and the objects of sense are their roads. The Self joined with the body, senses and mind is the enjoyer, say the wise.
1.3.5: But he (the charioteer, the intellect) who is without understanding, with the mind ever unrestrained — his senses are unruly, like the vicious horses of a charioteer.
1.3.6: And he who has understanding, with the mind ever restrained — his senses are obedient, like the good horses of a charioteer.
1.3.7: He who is without understanding, with the mind uncontrolled and ever impure, does not reach that goal, but goes on in the round of birth and death.
1.3.8: And he who has understanding, with the mind controlled and ever pure, reaches that goal from which he is not born again.
1.3.9: The man whose charioteer is understanding and who holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the road (of saṃsāra): that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu (the all-pervading).
1.3.10: Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; higher than the intellect is the great Self (the cosmic intellect).
1.3.11: Higher than the great is the unmanifest; higher than the unmanifest is the Puruṣa. Than the Puruṣa there is nothing higher: that is the end, that is the highest goal.
1.3.12: This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by those who see the subtle, with a keen and subtle intellect.
1.3.13: Let the wise man merge speech (and the senses) in the mind, and merge that (mind) in the knowing intellect; let him merge the intellect in the great Self, and merge that in the peaceful Self.
Speech in the mind: first speech and the other senses are stilled in the mind, then the mind in the intellect, the intellect in the cosmic intellect, and that in the supreme, peaceful Self (Śaṅkara).
1.3.14: Arise, awake; go to the best (teachers) and understand (the Self). The path is hard to tread, say the wise, like the sharpened edge of a razor, hard to cross.
1.3.15: Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal and odourless; without beginning or end, higher than the great, unchanging — having realised that, one is freed from the mouth of death.
1.3.16: Telling and hearing this eternal story of Naciketā, told by Death, the intelligent man is glorified in the world of Brahman.
1.3.17: He who, purified, recites this supreme secret in an assembly of brāhmaṇas, or at the time of a śrāddha, makes it bear endless fruit; it bears endless fruit.
The repeated sentence marks the end of the first adhyāya.
2.1.1: Yama said: The self-existent (Lord) made the senses outward-going; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self. Some wise man, desiring immortality, turned his eyes (his senses) back (from objects) and saw the inner Self.
2.1.2: The childish run after outward enjoyments; they fall into the widespread snare of death. But the wise, knowing immortality, do not seek the permanent here among impermanent things.
2.1.3: That by which one knows form, taste, smell, sounds, touches and the pleasures of union — by that very (Self) one knows (all this). What remains here (unknown by it)? This indeed is that.
'This indeed is that': this is the Self Naciketā asked about (1.2.14). The sentence is repeated at the end of several mantras that follow.
2.1.4: That by which one sees both the dream state and the waking state — knowing it as the great, all-pervading Self, the wise man does not grieve.
2.1.5: He who knows this Self close at hand (as himself), the eater of honey (the fruit of works), the bearer of life, the lord of the past and the future — thereafter he does not shrink (from anything). This indeed is that.
2.1.6: He who sees him (Hiraṇyagarbha) who was born before austerity (knowledge) and before the waters, who entered the cave (of the heart) and abides there, along with the elements (and the senses) — this indeed is that.
With Śaṅkara, 'before austerity' is read as born of Brahman before all else, at the beginning of creation: Hiraṇyagarbha, who dwells in the heart of beings.
2.1.7: She who comes to be as the vital breath (Hiraṇyagarbha), Aditi (the devourer of all), made of the gods, who entered the cave (of the heart) and abides there, who was born along with the elements — this indeed is that.
2.1.8: The fire (Jātavedas) hidden in the two fire-sticks, well guarded like a child in the womb by women with child, to be worshipped day after day by watchful men who bring offerings — this indeed is that.
2.1.9: That from which the sun rises and into which it sets — in that (the vital breath, the Self) all the gods are fixed; no one goes beyond it. This indeed is that.
2.1.10: What is here is there (in the other world); what is there is here too. He who sees as if there were difference here (in Brahman) goes from death to death.
2.1.11: By the (purified) mind alone is this to be attained; there is no difference here at all. He who sees as if there were difference here goes from death to death.
2.1.12: The Puruṣa (the Self), the size of a thumb, dwells in the middle of the body (in the heart), the lord of the past and the future. (Knowing him) one does not shrink thereafter. This indeed is that.
The size of a thumb: as measured by the heart in which it is seen; the Self itself is all-pervading (1.2.22).
2.1.13: The Puruṣa, the size of a thumb, is like a flame without smoke, the lord of the past and the future; he is today and he is tomorrow too. This indeed is that.
2.1.14: As water rained on a high place runs down the mountains in all directions, so he who sees the selves (the forms of the Self) as separate runs after them alone.
2.1.15: As pure water poured into pure water becomes just the same, so, Gautama, becomes the self of the sage who knows (the oneness).
2.2.1: The city of eleven gates (this body) belongs to the unborn one whose awareness is never crooked. Meditating on him, one does not grieve, and freed (from ignorance) one is liberated (when the body falls too). This indeed is that.
The eleven gates: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, the navel, the two lower openings and the opening at the crown of the head.
2.2.2: He is the swan (the sun) dwelling in the pure (heaven); the Vasu (the air) dwelling in the mid-region; the priest (fire) dwelling on the altar; the guest (Soma) dwelling in the house; dwelling in men, in the gods, in the truth (the sacrifice), in the sky; born in the waters, born of the earth, born of the sacrifice, born of the mountains (as rivers); the great truth.
This is a verse of the Ṛgveda (4.40.5). In every form it is the one Self.
2.2.3: He leads the up-breath upward and casts the down-breath inward; all the gods (the senses) worship the adorable dwarf (the Self) seated in the middle (in the heart).
The dwarf: the Self in its small (thumb-sized) form in the heart, worthy of worship. The gods are the senses, which bring him their objects as offerings.
2.2.4: When this embodied one, dwelling in the body, slips away and is released from the body, what remains here (in the body)? This indeed is that.
2.2.5: No mortal lives by the up-breath or by the down-breath. They live by another (the Self), on which these two depend.
2.2.6: Well then, Gautama, I shall tell you this secret, eternal Brahman, and also what becomes of the self (the soul) after it meets death.
2.2.7: Some embodied beings enter a womb to take a body; others pass into the unmoving (trees and the like), according to their deeds and according to their knowledge.
2.2.8: This Puruṣa who keeps awake among the sleeping, creating desire after desire (in dreams) — that alone is the pure, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal. In it all the worlds rest; no one goes beyond it. This indeed is that.
2.2.9: As the one fire, having entered the world, takes a form like every form, so the one inner Self of all beings takes a form like every form, and is outside (them) too.
2.2.10: As the one air, having entered the world, takes a form like every form, so the one inner Self of all beings takes a form like every form, and is outside (them) too.
2.2.11: As the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not tainted by the outer faults of the eyes, so the one inner Self of all beings is not tainted by the sorrow of the world, being outside it.
2.2.12: The one ruler, the inner Self of all beings, who makes his one form manifold — the wise who see him seated in their own self, theirs is everlasting happiness, not others'.
2.2.13: The eternal among the impermanent, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfils the desires of the many — the wise who see him seated in their own self, theirs is everlasting peace, not others'.
2.2.14: Naciketā said: That supreme bliss which (the wise) regard as 'this is that', and which cannot be described — how may I know it? Does it shine (of itself), or does it (only) reflect (another's light)?
2.2.15: Yama said: There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars, nor do these lightnings shine; how then this fire? When he shines, everything shines after him; by his light all this is lit.
2.3.1: This is the ancient aśvattha tree (of the world), with its root above (in Brahman) and its branches below. (Its root) alone is the pure, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal. In it all the worlds rest; no one goes beyond it. This indeed is that.
Aśvattha, 'that which does not stand till tomorrow': the fleeting world, whose root is above, in Brahman (compare Gītā 15.1).
2.3.2: Whatever this whole world is, it has come forth from the vital breath (Brahman) and moves in it. (That Brahman) is a great terror, like an upraised thunderbolt. Those who know this become immortal.
2.3.3: From fear of him fire burns; from fear the sun shines; from fear Indra and the wind (do their work); and death, the fifth, runs.
2.3.4: If one has been able to know him here, before the body falls away, (one is freed); otherwise one becomes fit to take a body (again) in the created worlds.
2.3.5: As in a mirror (clearly), so (is the Self seen) in one's own (purified) intellect; as in a dream (dimly), so in the world of the fathers; as it is seen in water (wavering), so in the world of the gandharvas; and as shade and sunlight (distinctly), so in the world of Brahmā.
2.3.6: Knowing the separateness (from the Self) of the senses, which arise separately, and their rising and setting, the wise man does not grieve.
2.3.7: Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; above the intellect is the great Self (the cosmic intellect); higher than the great is the unmanifest.
2.3.8: And higher than the unmanifest is the Puruṣa, all-pervading and without any mark, knowing whom a creature is freed and attains immortality.
2.3.9: His form does not stand within sight; no one sees him with the eye. He is revealed by the heart, by the intellect, by the mind (in meditation). Those who know this become immortal.
2.3.10: When the five senses come to rest together with the mind, and the intellect too does not stir, that they call the highest state.
2.3.11: That firm holding of the senses they regard as yoga. Then one is free from heedlessness, for yoga comes and goes.
Yoga comes and goes: the state of yoga arises and is lost, so one must remain watchful in it (Śaṅkara).
2.3.12: He cannot be reached by speech, nor by the mind, nor by the eye. How can he be apprehended, except from one who says 'he is'?
2.3.13: He is to be apprehended (first) as 'he is', and (then) in his true nature; of these two, for one who has apprehended him as 'he is', his true nature becomes clear.
2.3.14: When all the desires that dwell in his heart are let go, then the mortal becomes immortal; here (in this body) he attains Brahman.
2.3.15: When all the knots of the heart are cut asunder here, then the mortal becomes immortal. This much indeed is the teaching.
The knots of the heart: the bindings of ignorance such as 'I am this body' and 'this is mine'.
2.3.16: A hundred and one are the channels of the heart; of them one goes out towards the crown of the head. Going up by it, one attains immortality (the world of the gods); the others lead in various directions at the time of departing.
This is for the worshipper; the knower becomes Brahman here itself (2.3.14).
2.3.17: The Puruṣa, the inner Self, the size of a thumb, is ever seated in the heart of men. Let one draw him out of one's own body with steadiness, as the stalk from the muñja grass. Let one know him as the pure, the immortal; let one know him as the pure, the immortal.
The repeated sentence and the closing 'iti' mark the end of the Upaniṣad's teaching.
2.3.18: Then Naciketā, having received this knowledge told by Death and the whole method of yoga, attained Brahman, free of impurity (of merit and demerit) and free of death. So does any other who knows the inner Self in this way.
shanti.2: Om. May he (the Lord) protect us both together. May he nourish us both together. May we both gain strength together. May what we both have studied be full of light. May we never hate each other. Om, peace, peace, peace.
